newsitem.title: CANADA: Martin's spending targets children, research.
newsitem.headline: Martin's spending targets children, research.

text.p: The research community and children from poor families will be the main beneficiaries of Canada's 1997 budget.

Finance Minister Paul Martin announced new spending of C$600 million a year for low-income Canadian families under a new National Child Benefit System. The system, aimed at the working poor, will be fully implemented by July 1998, costing the federal government C$6.0 billion a year, most of which has already been committed.
As an interim measure, the government plans to increase its contributions to the Working Income Supplement by C$70 million in 1997 for a total of C$195 million for the year.

"Our children are our most precious resource and ensuring their health is our greatest responsibility," Martin said in his budget speech. "There can be no more worthy effort than a new partnership on behalf of Canada's children."

Martin also proposed spending C$800 million to start up a new five-year Canada Foundation for Innovation, designed to help fund research facilities and equipment at universities and research hospitals. The money will come from the 1996-97 budget and the foundation will spend proceeds from investing the C$800 million.
"It is a budget without further cuts to government programs," Martin said in his budget speech to Parliament.
New spending add up to approximately C$740 million in 1997/98, analysts said.

Total program spending in 1997-98 is expected to be C$105.8 billion or 12.7 percent of GDP, down from C$109 billion or 13.7 percent in 1996-97. In 1998-99, program spending should total C$103.5 billion or 11.9 percent of GDP.

"It's the lowest it's been since 1949-50 and it's probably one of the lowest in the G7 area," said senior economist Andrew Spence with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "So one has to say that the overall budget framework is one of super-credibility in the G7 context."

As part of his plan to create jobs, Martin also announced C$425 million in federal money on a national infrastructure program as well as C$50 million in 1997-98 to subsidize home renovations for low-income Canadians. These measures had been announced before Tuesday's budget.

The Canadian Tourism Commission will receive C$15 million a year over three years to promote Canada in foreign markets, and the government's Business Development Bank will receive $50 million to help finance private sector tourism, the government said.
The government will also inject $50 million into the Farm Credit Corp, and $10 million a year over three years into a program allowing rural Canadians to access the Internet.
The budget proposes adding C$137 million in 1998-99 and $202 million in 1999-2000 to federal assistance funds for higher education.

As for health care, the government proposes spending C$300 million over three years to improve the delivery of health services -- including C$150 million for pilot projects to try out government payment for prescription drugs and home care.
The government will also provide $30 million a year over three years for a fund to help Canadians with disabilities integrate into their communities.
